items.stem:
Study the table related to colour change with indicators and answer the questions that follow.
SolutionsColour change with phenolphthalein indicatorColour change with methyl orange indicator
PPinkYellow
QColourlessOrange
RColourlessRed
(i) Name the solution which is acidic. (ii) Arrange the given solutions in increasing order of their pH value. (iii) What is the name of solution P and Q? (iv) When solution P is added to the China rose indicator, what is the colour of solution P?
items.answer:
(i) Solution R is acidic because it changes to red on adding methyl orange indicator.
(ii) R < Q < P
(iii) Solution P and Q could be NaOH and NaCl.
(iv) Green.
items.ocr: Section heading printed as 'CASE BASED QUEATIONS' (typo in source); normalised to 'CASE BASED QUESTIONS'. OCR spellings repaired: 'soution' -> 'solution', 'chima rose' -> 'China rose'. Printed key is self-contradictory: part (i) identifies R as the acidic solution (so R has the lowest pH) and the table makes P the basic one, yet part (ii) prints the increasing-pH order as 'P < Q < R', that order reversed. Following the chapter convention that the worked reasoning outranks a bare key, part (ii) is stored as 'R < Q < P'; the printed string is recorded here.

items.stem:
When the rain water contains large quantities of acids like nitric acid and sulphuric acid formed by dissolution of oxides of nitrogen and sulphur in water it is called as P. Q is formed of acidic water received on soil through rain, fog and snow. R is formed of wind-blown acidic gases and particles in the atmosphere which fall on ground with rain water.

(i) Identify the labelled parts as P, Q and R in this passage.
(ii) Among P, Q and R, which part is mainly responsible for half of acidity in atmosphere that comes to earth?
items.answer:
(i) In the given passage, P, Q and R are acid rain, wet deposition and dry deposition respectively.
(ii) About half of the acidity in the atmosphere comes to earth through dry deposition (R).
items.ocr: Only two sub-parts are printed for this case; marks kept at 4 as per the CASE BASED section. Printed answer (ii) reads 'comes to earth through i.e., dry deposition (R)' - the stray 'i.e.,' removed.

items.stem:
Acids, bases and salts are three main categories of chemical compounds. These have certain definite properties which distinguish one class from the other. The acids are sour in taste while bases are bitter in taste. Tasting a substance is not a good way of finding out if it is an acid or a base! Acids and bases can be better distinguished with the help of indicators. Indicators are substances that undergo a change of colour with a change of acidic, neutral or basic medium. Many of these indicators are derived from natural substances such as extracts from flower petals and bark. Litmus, a purple dye, is extracted from the lichen plant. Some indicators are prepared artificially. For example, methyl orange and phenolphthalein. Given below is a table of indicators and their colour change in acidic and basic medium.
IndicatorColour in AcidColour in Alkali
LitmusRedBlue
MethylPinkish redYellow
PhenolphthaleinColourlessPink
(i) Give two examples each of natural and artificial indicators. (ii) An aqueous solution turns red litmus solution blue. Excess addition of which solution would reverse the change - ammonium hydroxide solution or hydrochloric acid? (iii) What will be the change in colour when a few drops of phenolphthalein is added to a solution having pH 8.5? (iv) What is universal indicator?
items.answer:
(i) Natural indicators: turmeric and red cabbage. Artificial indicators: methyl red and methyl orange.
(ii) Hydrochloric acid, because adding excess acid to the base would turn blue litmus solution red.
(iii) It changes to pink.
(iv) Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes that changes colour gradually over a range of pH and is used in testing for acids and alkalis.
items.ocr: Passage word 'barrier' repaired to 'bark' (source reads 'flower petals and barrier'). Table row label printed as 'Methyl' only - kept verbatim; it refers to methyl orange.

items.stem:
The pH scale can be used to determine the strength of acid solutions as well as basic solutions by making use of hydrogen ion concentrations in them. Consider two solutions A and B having pH values 3 and 9.5, respectively.

(i) Which solution will turn blue litmus red?
(ii) Which solution will turn phenolphthalein from colourless to pink?
(iii) Water is a neutral substance. What colour will you get when you add a few drops of universal indicator to a test tube containing distilled water?
items.answer:
(i) Solution A will turn blue litmus to red as its value of pH is 3.
(ii) Solution B will turn phenolphthalein from colourless to pink as it is basic in nature.
(iii) It turns the universal indicator solution green as its pH value is 7.
items.ocr: Only three sub-parts are printed for this case; marks kept at 4 as per the CASE BASED section.

items.stem:
A metal carbonate X on heating with an acid gives a gas which when passed through a solution Y gives the carbonate back. On the other hand, a gas G that is obtained at anode during electrolysis of brine is passed on dry Y, it gives a compound Z, used for disinfecting drinking water.

(i) Identify X, Y, G and Z.
(ii) What is the nature of the gas evolved when X is heated?
(iii) Write the reaction involved in the formation of G.
(iv) Write the reaction involved when G reacts with Y.
items.answer:
(i) X is calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Y is slaked lime [Ca(OH)₂]. G is chlorine (Cl₂) gas. Z is bleaching powder (CaOCl₂).
(ii) CaCO₃(s) —Δ→ CaO(s) + CO₂(g). The gas CO₂ is acidic in nature.
(iii) 2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl₂(g) + H₂(g)
(iv) Cl₂(g) + Ca(OH)₂(s) → CaOCl₂(s) + H₂O(l)
items.ocr: LaTeX in the worked solution rewritten to Unicode; MinerU had split the formulae from their subscripts ('^CaCO h. 3' -> CaCO₃, '^Cl 2 h' -> Cl₂, '^CaOCl h. 2' -> CaOCl₂) and wrapped the brine electrolysis equation in an array environment whose reaction arrow (\longrightarrow) was restored as →. Heating arrow \xrightarrow{\Delta} rendered as —Δ→.

items.stem:
Baking soda is used in small amounts for making bread and cakes. It helps to make these soft and spongy. An aqueous solution of baking soda turns red litmus blue. It is also used in soda acid fire extinguisher. Use this information to answer the following questions.

(i) Write the equation for the reaction between baking soda and acid.
(ii) How does it help in extinguishing fire?
(iii) What is the reaction involved when it is heated?
(iv) Is the pH value of baking soda solution lower than or higher than 7?
items.answer:
(i) The equation for the reaction is
2NaHCO₃(s) [Baking soda] + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l) + 2CO₂(g)
(ii) The CO₂ gas produced by the reaction of baking soda and acid in the soda-acid fire extinguisher helps in extinguishing fire.
(iii) The reaction involved is
2NaHCO₃(s) —Δ→ Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)↑
(iv) The pH value of baking soda solution is higher than 7, i.e. it is alkaline.
items.ocr: LaTeX rewritten to Unicode; the '^Baking sodah' label artefact (a broken \underbrace caption) restored as the bracketed label [Baking soda]. Printed answer (iv) reads 'in higher than 7' - corrected to 'is higher than 7'.

items.stem:
A dry pellet of a common base B when kept in open absorbs moisture and turns sticky. The compound is also a by-product of chlor-alkali process.

(i) What is the name of B?
(ii) What type of reaction occurs when B is treated with an acid?
(iii) Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of B with CO₂.
(iv) Which gas is evolved when B reacts with Zn?
items.answer:
(i) B is sodium hydroxide (NaOH).
(ii) Neutralisation reaction occurs when B is treated with an acid.
(iii) The chemical reaction is 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O
(iv) Hydrogen gas is evolved. The chemical reaction is 2NaOH + Zn → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂
items.ocr: Printed answer (i) reads 'B is solution hydroxide (NaOH)' - OCR of 'sodium hydroxide', repaired from the formula given alongside. Stem typo 'evloved' -> 'evolved'. LaTeX equations rewritten to Unicode with the reaction arrow restored as →. Printed answer (iv) gave only the equation; the named gas (hydrogen) added from that equation.

(b) The line 'Answer the questions giving examples in each case.' was extracted into a stray '> **Answer**' blockquote between the stem and the sub-questions; it is part of the question and has been folded into the stem. (c) The HTML table was emitted AFTER the answer key in the markdown; it has been moved back into the stem where it is printed. (d) The table is kept VERBATIM and is itself damaged: the serial-number column is empty for rows 1-4, the row for substance C has lost both its label and its pH value (only 'Dard red', i.e. 'Dark red', survives) and the row for substance D has lost its label. The answer key confirms C is the strong acid (dark red) and D is the pH 8.5 greenish-blue baking soda. (e) 'vinager' -> 'vinegar'. items.stem:
Children eat a lot of sugary foods such as cakes, pastries, chocolates etc. which can lead to tooth decay. Tooth decay is the gradual destruction of hard outer tissues of the tooth that leads to the formation of cavities or caries in tooth. Whenever we eat any food, some of the food particles stick in-between our teeth. The bacteria present in our mouth break down the sugar present in the food to form acid. This acid changes the pH of the mouth which may be the main cause of tooth decay.

[Figure: pH scale from 1.0 to 14.0 marked Acidic at the left and Alkaline at the right, with an arrow pointing to 5.5]

(i) What is meant by saying that pH change may be the main cause of tooth decay?
(ii) What is the critical pH at which tooth decay starts?
(iii) The nature of the toothpaste used for cleaning teeth is ______.
(iv) Based on the data shown in the graph below, which of the two children A and B would have more teeth with cavities and why?

[Graph: Dental cavities in percentage (%) against Months (Jan-Dec) for Child A (dashed) and Child B (solid)]
items.answer:
(i) Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth falls below 5.5. The acid then becomes strong enough to corrode the hard enamel of the tooth.
(ii) 5.5
(iii) Basic
(iv) Child B. Eating lots of chocolates, chips or candies leads to tooth cavity.

Both are attached. Sub-part (iii) is printed as an incomplete sentence ('The nature of the toothpaste used for cleaning teeth is') - a blank was added to show it is a fill-in.
